newsitem.title: USA: Simpson confronted with ex-wife's letter.
newsitem.headline: Simpson confronted with ex-wife's letter.

text.p: O.J. Simpson, testifying in his civil trial on Monday, was confronted with a letter written by his ex-wife in which she said she stopped loving him on Jan. 1, 1989, when he allegedly beat her.
Nicole Brown Simpson also wrote in the undated letter, "I'd like you to keep this letter if we split so you will always know why we split."
Of the 1989 incident she wrote: "I have never loved you since."
Asked about that by Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead attorney in the case, Simpson replied, "She told me just the opposite."
Simpson said his ex-wife told him her lawyers "had her write up various things for our divorce, but she would not testify to them, in her deposition or in court." The two divorced in 1992.

After being asked by his defence attorney, Robert Baker, "On June 12, 1994, did you, with your children at home upstairs, murder your ex-wife and leave her body there for the kids to find?" and firmly answering, "Absolutely not," Simpson ended his testimony after one-and-a-half days on the witness stand.

In arguing that the letter and Nicole Brown Simpson's diary be admitted in evidence during his cross-examination of Simpson, Petrocelli told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki that in the diary entry referring to the alleged beating she wrote, "He beat the holy hell out of me." The judge allowed the items in to show Nicole Brown Simpson's state of mind.

Later Petrocelli confronted Simpson with several new photographs of the ex-football player at a Buffalo Bills game in 1993 in which he is apparently wearing Bruno Magli designer shoes similar to ones FBI experts say left a bloody footprint at the murder scene.
Simpson denied ever owning such shoes and told Petrocelli that he didn't think the pants he was wearing in the pictore were authentic either.
"I'm normally a pretty sharp dresser and they (pants) don't look like me. They don't look like they fit," Simpson said.
His defence has argued that a previous photo of Simpson at the game and apparently wearing such shoes, was doctored.
Petrocelli then told him: "You lied to this jury when you said you weren't wearing those shoes, didn't you?" Simpson said "No."

Earlier Simpson told Baker he contemplated suicide during the famous slow-speed freeway chase on the day he was due to surrender to police and was charged with the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife and her friend Ronald Goldman.
"I was feeling a lot of pain ... I just wanted to go to Nicole's grave. I was feeling, I guess, suicidal. I just wanted my pain to end," he said.

Simpson, who was acquitted of the murders by a criminal court jury in October 1995 and is now battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims, choked up at one point during Monday's testimony when he described asking police in a telephone call from his Chicago hotel room if his young children, Sydney and Justin, were safe.

"I wanted to know if my kids had been exposed to anything and he (Det. Ron Phillips) said 'No,' that they had been taken out the back (of Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium) and they didn't see anything," Simpson said in a breaking voice.
The two victims were stabbed and slashed to death on the front walkway of the condominium.

Simpson, losing his composure for the first time in nearly four days on the witness stand, including two-and-a-half days in November, was given a glass of water and breathed deeply before continuing. He said Phillips had told him his ex-wife had been murdered and he learned there was a second victim from his eldest daughter from a previous marriage, Arnelle.

Talking about visiting his ex-wife's grave on June 17, when he was supposed to surrender, he said he was driven to the cemetery south of Los Angeles by his close friend, Al "A.C." Cowlings, but they were unable to get to the gravesite because a police car was parked at the entrance.
He said the two sat in a nearby orange grove and he got in the back seat of the car and took out a gun.

Asked why he did not go through with killing himself, he replied, "A.C., and my mom told me years ago that you can't go to heaven if you commit suicide and I was dealing with that, and thank God for A.C."
The defence was expected to rest its case on Tuesday.
